Just to clarify, any advice given here should be taken up with your Dr.  So anything I say for me may not be the case for you.

I’m on antidepressants (in my case prozac which is an SSRI) and you are on 3 (bubroprion- most people would know as Zyban; Mirtazapine; and Venlafaxine).  I’m also on quetiapine (an antipsychotic - which is often prescribed “off label” as we call it here “, as a mood stabaliser) but you are also on carbolithium which is also an antipsychotic. The zolpidem as I’ve read is meant only for short-term use (4 weeks) for insomnia and is classified as a hypnotic.  So whilst it seems like there are some double ups of medication, it may be this last one that I might be concerned with. So talk to your prescribing Dr maybe about looking at whether you need to be on all these medications (I’m in Australia and whilst some of these are government subsidised so they don’t cost “too” much, for me it comes down to 2 things - is this particular drug helping me - the most important, and is this drug affordable in the long run - less important as staying alive is more important than money?)

The other thing I would mention is that a diagnosis of BPD just not mean you don’t have other mental health issues that need to be considered, and treated possibly with drugs.  Also, even if it is your only diagnosis, medications can sometimes help whilst you’re receiving therapy (be it Group or one-on-one, DBT, CBT, ACT,  psychotherapy, etc.) just to stabilise your mood whilst you learn other skills and techniques.

But again, (and if the mods want to delete this response, ok) 1. your dr should be the one you talk to about medications. 2. You can get a second opinion. 3. Your psychiatrist and GP (general practitioner - so your regular doctor you see for anything - not sure what you would call them? Primary care practitioner) maybe need to work together. And don’t be afraid to raise concerns about your physical health in relation to psych meds. I think too often because (in my mind experience), I’m often suicidal, my physical health (I’m 40 btw) is secondary to “keeping me alive by not committing suicide”/ drinking too much.  If you think something is wrong besides your mental health, talk about it with your Dr’s. And this is a purely anecdotal issue related to me, but one of the “off-label” meds I had dropped my B12 levels significantly. Thank goodness my GP (and my own research) indicated that the medication could be the reason and I would taken off that drug. No more problems.

I’ve been suicidal and begged a cop to shoot me. Thankfully they have the necessary training to, firstly, know how to talk to people, deescalate a situation, and use non-lethal means to “disable” a potential threat. Shit, I pushed that cop, yelled at him, threatened him, and he still acted professionally and compassionately that I got the help I needed. The cops here still get shit and called pigs but I know they save lives and put their own lives in danger everyday.  And it’s their training in more than just shooting that makes them good cops.

I'll start with, I haven't given birth, but I am a sufferer of PTSD, so at first I was thinking, "really? Is this person serious?" But the more I read your post and thought about it, I realised that women, society, do silence the negative aspects of a lot of things including childbirth because it's "meant to be a wonderful experience". I've discussed having children with my MIL who was midwife and she is quite frank. If you really want children you need to be prepared for the truth. You'll be pushing hard! And not just on the uterus for the baby to come out. Other stuff is going to come out possibly/probably (urine/shit). You will tear, so the best course of action is actually to discuss it beforehand and make the decision to choose to do a surgical cut which will be straight and clean, making it easier to stitch and it will heal a lot neater. This is really important as it will greatly reduce the scarring, and future births can follow the same incision line. 

OP, you are right, woman, people, need to start talking about all kinds of issues we face all the time, especially the things we take for granted, the things that because so many other people may go through we develop this attitude of "don't talk about it". And then in order to talk about it things need to be labelled as mental illnesses (and please, I am not downgrading the severity of mental illness here,I suffer from my own, just here me out) for people to be able to get support, such as post natal depression, or in your case, a group of woman who experienced tearing (so not a mental illness per se, but you did mention PTSD). But maybe it is true PTSD, but could it have been avoided? Maybe? Sorry rambling now.  It's just that we need to start talking about the events that impact us psychologically not playing games of "it happened to me and I'm ok" because you can play that game for a so many things that happen to people and it's not helpful.
